about: Topic map of the AP Physics 1 Course and Exam Description (2024-25 revision), written in LevlPrep's own words from docs/apphys-research/framework.md. No CED text is reproduced. Units 1-2 objectives and exclusions were read in the CED; Units 3-8 come from a per-topic transcription and must be verified (docs/apphys-needs-author.md, ced-exclusions); Unit 7 topic names are unverified (unit7-names).

ced.title: AP Physics 1: Algebra-Based Course and Exam Description
ced.effective: Fall 2024; first exam May 2025; May 2027 timing per the fall 2026 clarifications
ced.verification: CED PDF text read through the Unit 3 opener; topic names for every unit from the Course at a Glance except Unit 7.
ced.oldNamesWarning: Pre-2024 resources have 7 units, include waves, sound and circuits, and used 5 FRQs with multi-select MCQ; do not copy their numbering.

skillNames.1.A: Create diagrams, tables, charts or schematics of a physical situation
skillNames.1.B: Create quantitative graphs with scales, units and plotted data
skillNames.1.C: Sketch qualitative graphs of how a model behaves

skillNames.2.A: Derive a symbolic expression from known quantities
skillNames.2.B: Calculate or estimate a quantity, with units
skillNames.2.C: Compare quantities across scenarios, times or places
skillNames.2.D: Predict new values or factors of change from functional dependence

skillNames.3.A: Design an experimental procedure for a question
skillNames.3.B: Apply a law, definition or model to make a claim
skillNames.3.C: Justify a claim with evidence, representations or principles

sciencePracticesNote: Practices are not tied to learning objectives: any objective can be tested with any skill. Exam weights by practice are from a third-party copy of the CED table [unverified]; MCQ is mostly Mathematical Routines, and Creating Representations is assessed in free response (practice 1 is free response only here).

topics.title: Scalars and Vectors on a Line
objectives: Tell scalars from vectors and add vectors that lie along one line.
knowledge: A scalar has only a size; a vector has a size and a direction.
Distance and speed are scalars; position, displacement, velocity and acceleration are vectors.
Along one line, the sign of a vector gives its direction; opposite directions get opposite signs.

topics.title: Displacement, Velocity and Acceleration
objectives: Describe motion with displacement, average velocity and average acceleration.
knowledge: Displacement is the change in position; an object model ignores size, shape and inner structure.
Average velocity is Δx/Δt and average acceleration is Δv/Δt.
An object accelerates when its speed or its direction changes; averages over short intervals approach instantaneous values.

topics.title: Representing Motion
objectives: Move between motion diagrams, graphs, equations and words for one-dimensional motion.
knowledge: Three equations describe constant acceleration.
Near Earth a freely falling object accelerates downward at g, about 10 m/s² (9.8 m/s² is also accepted).
Slope of x-t is velocity, slope of v-t is acceleration, area under v-t is displacement, area under a-t is change in velocity.
exclusions: Nonuniform acceleration is handled only qualitatively (graphs and words), never with calculations.

topics.title: Reference Frames and Relative Motion
objectives: Describe the same motion from two inertial frames.
knowledge: Every measurement of motion is made by an observer in some reference frame.
Velocity seen by an observer = velocity of the object in another frame + velocity of that frame.
Acceleration is the same in every inertial frame.
exclusions: Relative velocity is added only in one dimension.
Frames are inertial unless a question says otherwise.

topics.title: Vectors and Motion in Two Dimensions
objectives: Resolve vectors into components and treat two-dimensional motion as two independent one-dimensional motions.
knowledge: Any vector can be split into perpendicular components with trigonometry, in a coordinate system you choose.
Perpendicular components of motion are independent.
A projectile has zero acceleration horizontally and constant acceleration vertically.

topics.title: Systems and Center of Mass
objectives: Choose a system and find its center of mass.
knowledge: A system's behavior comes from the interactions inside it; when the inside does not matter it can be treated as one object.
The center of mass lies on any line of symmetry; x_cm = Σmx/Σm.
A system can be modelled as a point at its center of mass.
exclusions: Center of mass is calculated only for five or fewer point objects in two dimensions, or for highly symmetric objects.

topics.title: Forces and Free-Body Diagrams
objectives: Identify the forces on an object and draw its free-body diagram.
knowledge: A force is an interaction between two objects; an object cannot exert a net force on itself.
Contact forces are electric forces between surfaces at the large scale.
A free-body diagram shows every force the surroundings exert on the object, drawn from a dot at its center of mass.
exclusions: Free-body diagrams show whole forces, never their components.

topics.title: Newton's Third Law
objectives: Pair forces between interacting objects and treat strings and pulleys as ideal.
knowledge: The two forces of an interaction are equal in size, opposite in direction and act on different objects.
Internal forces do not change the motion of the center of mass.
An ideal string is massless and does not stretch, with one tension along it; an ideal pulley is massless and frictionless.
exclusions: Tension in a string or chain with mass is qualitative only.
Gravity is the only force at a distance in this course.

topics.title: Newton's First Law
objectives: Relate balanced forces to constant velocity.
knowledge: The net force is the vector sum of all forces on an object.
Zero net force means constant velocity (translational equilibrium); forces can balance in one direction and not in another.
An inertial reference frame is one in which the first law holds.

topics.title: Newton's Second Law
objectives: Use net force and mass to find acceleration.
knowledge: The center-of-mass acceleration is proportional to the net external force and in its direction.
Only a nonzero net external force changes the velocity of the center of mass.

topics.title: Gravitational Force
objectives: Use Newton's law of gravitation and relate weight, apparent weight and the gravitational field.
knowledge: Gravitational force ∝ m1m2/r², attractive, along the line between centers.
The gravitational field g = F/m; near a planet's surface it is treated as constant.
Apparent weight is the normal force; it differs from mg when the object accelerates.
Inertial and gravitational mass are found by experiment to be equal.

topics.title: Kinetic and Static Friction
objectives: Model kinetic and static friction.
knowledge: Kinetic friction is μk·F_N, opposes the sliding of the surfaces, and does not depend on contact area.
Static friction takes whatever value prevents slipping, up to μs·F_N; usually μs > μk.
The normal force is perpendicular to the surface and away from it.

topics.title: Spring Forces
objectives: Use Hooke's law for an ideal spring.
knowledge: An ideal spring is massless; its force is F = −kΔx, always toward its relaxed length.

topics.title: Circular Motion
objectives: Analyze objects moving in circles, including circular orbits.
knowledge: Centripetal acceleration is v²/r toward the center, supplied by one force, several, or components of forces.
Tangential acceleration changes speed; total acceleration is the vector sum.
Period T = 2πr/v; frequency is 1/T.
Circular orbits link the period and the radius through the central mass (Kepler's third law).
exclusions: Banked curves are quantitative only when no friction is needed; with friction they are qualitative.
Kepler's first and second laws are not required.

topics.title: Translational Kinetic Energy
objectives: Calculate kinetic energy and compare it across situations.
knowledge: K = ½mv², a scalar that is never negative.
Kinetic energy depends on the reference frame.

topics.title: Work
objectives: Find the work done by a force and use the work-energy theorem.
knowledge: Work is energy transferred by a force; it can be positive, negative or zero.
For a constant force only the component parallel to the displacement does work.
The net work equals the change in kinetic energy; work is the area under a force-position graph.
exclusions: Only mechanical energy transfer is analyzed (no heating or thermodynamics).

topics.title: Potential Energy
objectives: Define potential energy for a system and calculate it for springs and gravity.
knowledge: Potential energy belongs to a system of interacting objects and exists only for conservative forces.
The zero point is chosen; ΔU_g = mgΔy, U_s = ½k(Δx)², U_G = −Gm1m2/r.

topics.title: Conservation of Energy
objectives: Track energy in a system with bar charts and equations.
knowledge: A single-object system has only kinetic energy.
Mechanical energy = K + U; it changes only by work from outside or by internal nonconservative forces.
Total energy is always conserved.
exclusions: Energy dissipated as thermal energy or sound is described qualitatively; only mechanical energy is analyzed quantitatively.

topics.title: Power
objectives: Calculate average and instantaneous power.
knowledge: Average power = ΔE/Δt = W/Δt.
Instantaneous power = F∥·v.

topics.title: Linear Momentum
objectives: Calculate momentum and use the collision and explosion models.
knowledge: p = mv, a vector in the direction of the velocity.
In a collision or explosion the internal forces are much larger than any external force.
exclusions: "Momentum" means linear momentum unless a question says otherwise.

topics.title: Change in Momentum and Impulse
objectives: Relate impulse to change in momentum, including from graphs.
knowledge: Impulse J = F_avg·Δt is a vector and the area under a force-time graph.
Impulse equals the change in momentum; net force is the slope of a momentum-time graph.
exclusions: No quantitative analysis of systems whose mass changes (rockets, leaking carts).

topics.title: Conservation of Linear Momentum
objectives: Decide when momentum is conserved and use conservation in one dimension.
knowledge: With no net external force the center-of-mass velocity and the total momentum stay constant.
Whether momentum changes depends on the system chosen.
exclusions: No questions that need simultaneous equations.
Momentum conservation is quantitative in one dimension; two dimensions are semiquantitative only.

topics.title: Elastic and Inelastic Collisions
objectives: Classify collisions by what happens to kinetic energy.
knowledge: Elastic: total kinetic energy is unchanged (each object's can change).
Inelastic: total kinetic energy decreases; perfectly inelastic: the objects stick and share one final velocity.
exclusions: No simultaneous equations (no "find both final velocities" of an elastic collision).

topics.title: Rotational Kinematics
objectives: Describe rotation about a fixed axis with angular quantities.
knowledge: Angular displacement (in radians), angular velocity and angular acceleration describe a rigid system turning about a fixed axis.
Three constant-α equations and their graphs mirror one-dimensional kinematics.
exclusions: Rotation is described only as clockwise or counterclockwise about a given axis (no vector directions).

topics.title: Linking Linear and Rotational Motion
objectives: Connect a point's linear motion to the rotation of the body.
knowledge: s = rθ, v = rω, a_T = rα.
Every point of a rigid body shares the same ω and α.
exclusions: Clockwise or counterclockwise only.

topics.title: Torque
objectives: Calculate torque and draw force diagrams that show where forces act.
knowledge: Only the force component perpendicular to r produces torque; the lever arm is the perpendicular distance from the axis to the line of action.
τ = rF sinθ.
exclusions: The direction of the torque vector is beyond scope (sign conventions only).

topics.title: Rotational Inertia
objectives: Find rotational inertia from how mass is spread around the axis.
knowledge: I = Σmr² for point masses; it depends on mass and its distribution.
I is least about the center of mass; I' = I_cm + Md².
exclusions: Calculate I for at most five objects; I of disks, rods and spheres is given, never memorized.

topics.title: Rotational Equilibrium
objectives: Use zero net torque and zero net force to analyze balanced objects.
knowledge: Rotational and translational equilibrium are independent conditions.
Zero net torque means constant angular velocity; an unbalanced torque changes it.
exclusions: No rotation in more than one plane at once.

topics.title: Newton's Second Law for Rotation
objectives: Use α = τ_net/I, alone or with translational analysis.
knowledge: Angular acceleration is net torque divided by rotational inertia, in the direction of the net torque.
A full description may need separate translational and rotational analyses.

units.title: Energy and Momentum of Rotating Systems

topics.title: Rotational Kinetic Energy
objectives: Calculate rotational kinetic energy.
knowledge: K_rot = ½Iω², a scalar; a spinning body can have it while its center of mass is at rest.

topics.title: Torque and Work
objectives: Find the work done by a torque.
knowledge: W = τΔθ; the area under a torque-angle graph.

topics.title: Angular Momentum and Angular Impulse
objectives: Calculate angular momentum and relate angular impulse to its change.
knowledge: L = Iω for a rigid body; L = rmv sinθ for a point object about a chosen point.
Angular impulse τΔt equals ΔL; net torque is the slope of an L-t graph.
exclusions: The direction of angular momentum and angular impulse is beyond scope.

topics.title: Conservation of Angular Momentum
objectives: Use conservation of angular momentum when shape changes.
knowledge: Total L is the sum of the parts; changing shape at constant L changes ω.
L is conserved when the net external torque is zero; the system choice matters.

topics.title: Rolling
objectives: Analyze objects that roll with and without slipping.
knowledge: Total kinetic energy = translational + rotational.
Rolling without slipping links v_cm = rω; static friction does no dissipative work.
Rolling while slipping has no such link and kinetic friction dissipates energy.
exclusions: Rolling friction is beyond scope.
Rolling while slipping is qualitative only.

topics.title: Motion of Orbiting Satellites
objectives: Use energy and angular momentum for circular and elliptical orbits.
knowledge: In a circular orbit E, U, K and L are all constant; in an elliptical orbit E and L are constant while U and K change.
U_G = 0 at infinite separation; escape speed comes from total energy = 0.
exclusions: Kepler's first and second laws are not required.

topics.title: Defining Simple Harmonic Motion
objectives: Recognize simple harmonic motion from its restoring force.
knowledge: SHM is periodic motion with a restoring force proportional to the displacement and opposite to it.
Equilibrium is where the net force is zero.
A pendulum at small angles is close to SHM.

topics.title: Frequency and Period of SHM
objectives: Find what the period of a spring-mass system or a pendulum depends on.
knowledge: Spring-mass: T = 2π√(m/k); small-angle pendulum: T = 2π√(ℓ/g).

topics.title: Representing and Analyzing SHM
objectives: Describe SHM with sine or cosine functions and graphs.
knowledge: x(t) is a sine or cosine of time; maxima, minima and zeros of x, v and a are related.
The period does not depend on the amplitude.

topics.title: Energy of Simple Harmonic Oscillators
objectives: Track kinetic and potential energy through an oscillation.
knowledge: E = K + U stays constant; K is largest where U is smallest.
The amplitude sets the total energy (E = ½kA² for a spring).

topics.title: Internal Structure and Density
objectives: Describe fluids and calculate density.
knowledge: States of matter differ in how their particles interact; a fluid has no fixed shape.
ρ = m/V; an ideal fluid is incompressible and has no viscosity.

topics.title: Pressure
objectives: Calculate pressure and how it changes with depth.
knowledge: P = F⊥/A is a scalar.
Fluid pressure comes from particle collisions; P = P0 + ρgh, and gauge pressure is ρgh.

topics.title: Fluids and Newton's Laws
objectives: Apply Newton's laws to fluids and to objects in them, including buoyancy.
knowledge: Newton's laws apply to a parcel of fluid.
The buoyant force is the net upward push of the fluid; F_b = ρ_fluid·V_displaced·g.

topics.title: Fluids and Conservation Laws
objectives: Use continuity and Bernoulli's equation for flowing fluids.
knowledge: Volume flow rate Av is constant along a full pipe: A1v1 = A2v2.
Bernoulli's equation is energy conservation for a fluid; Torricelli's result follows from it.
exclusions: Unless stated, fluids are ideal and pipes are completely full (no viscosity, turbulence or compressibility).

skillsTopics.title: Units, Prefixes and Significant Figures
objectives: Carry SI units through every calculation and convert between prefixes.
knowledge: Every measured quantity is a number with a unit.
Metric prefixes scale a unit by powers of ten (centi 10⁻², milli 10⁻³, kilo 10³).
Report a calculated result to the significant figures the data support.

skillsTopics.title: Rearranging Equations with Symbols
objectives: Solve an equation for any variable and keep answers in symbols.
knowledge: Δ means "final minus initial".
Do the same operation to both sides to isolate a variable; substitute numbers last.

skillsTopics.title: Proportional Reasoning and Functional Dependence
objectives: Predict how one quantity changes when another is scaled.
knowledge: y ∝ x: doubling x doubles y; y ∝ 1/x: doubling x halves y; y ∝ x²: doubling x quadruples y.
Read the factor of change straight from an equation.

skillsTopics.title: Slopes and Areas of Graphs
objectives: Read slopes and areas of graphs and turn a curve into a straight line.
knowledge: Slope = rise/run, with units of y over units of x.
Area under a graph has units of y times units of x.
Plotting the right combination of variables gives a straight line whose slope means something.

skillsTopics.title: Right-Triangle Trigonometry and Vector Components
objectives: Split a vector into components with sine and cosine.
knowledge: In a right triangle: sin = opposite/hypotenuse, cos = adjacent/hypotenuse, tan = opposite/adjacent.
A vector of size A at angle θ to the x-axis has components A cosθ and A sinθ.
Check that the calculator is in degree mode.

verifiedUnits1to2: 2.1 center of mass beyond five objects or symmetric systems
2.2 force components drawn on a free-body diagram
2.3 quantitative tension in massive strings; forces at a distance other than gravity
2.9 friction-required banked curves (quantitative); Kepler's first and second laws
unverifiedUnits3to8: 5.1-5.3 vector directions of rotation and torque
5.4 memorizing I of extended bodies; more than five objects
5.5 rotation in more than one plane
6.5 rolling friction; quantitative rolling while slipping
8.4 nonideal fluids and partly filled pipes
outOfCourse: mechanical waves and sound (moved to AP Physics 2)

exam.delivery: Hybrid digital in Bluebook: multiple choice on screen; free-response questions read on screen and handwritten in paper booklets.

mcq.format: Single-select only; discrete items and sets that share a stimulus.

exam.calculator: Allowed on both sections; Desmos built into Bluebook.
exam.reference: Equations sheet with g = 9.8 m/s² (10 m/s² accepted). Not on it: moments of inertia of shapes (given in questions), escape speed, Torricelli, Kepler's third law.
exam.previousFormat: 2025 and 2026: 40 MCQ in 80 min, 4 FRQs in 100 min.

changes2024: Fluids moved in as Unit 8; waves and sound moved out; science practices cut from 7 to 3; multi-select MCQ removed; four new FRQ types.
